title: Mathematics: Unit-wise Objective Question Bank
html:
Group A of the NEB Grade 11 Mathematics paper is eleven one-mark multiple-choice questions, taken from across the twenty-one chapters of the syllabus. Eleven marks, and none of them needs more than a minute if you have the right fact ready. This chapter drills every chapter in syllabus order: each section gives five to eight practice MCQs, then an answer key in which every answer carries a one-line reason, and names the misconception where a wrong option is a real trap.

What Group A actually tests

An MCQ in Mathematics is almost never a long calculation. It tests a formula you must recall, a single substitution, a definition or property, or a common slip (a sign, a missing factor of 2, a wrong quadrant) offered as a distractor. If a question is taking you more than ninety seconds, step back and look for the shortcut.

Practice items, not past papers

Every question below is an original practice item built from the public CDC syllabus. None is labelled with an examination year, because we cannot verify any item against an officially released paper. Use the bank for exam-shaped practice, not as a leaked list.

11.1 Logic and Set

  1. The negation of the statement "All students are present" is [1]aNo student is presentbSome student is absentcSome student is presentdAll students are absent
  2. The implication p \Rightarrow q is false only when [1]ap true, q truebp true, q falsecp false, q truedp false, q false
  3. The contrapositive of p \Rightarrow q is [1]aq \Rightarrow pb\sim p \Rightarrow \sim qc\sim q \Rightarrow \sim pd\sim q \Rightarrow p
  4. If n(A)=20, n(B)=15 and n(A\cap B)=5, then n(A\cup B) is [1]a40b35c30d25
  5. By De Morgan's law, (A\cup B)' equals [1]aA'\cup B'bA'\cap B'cA\cap BdA\cup B'
  6. The compound statement p \wedge \sim p is always [1]aa tautologybtrueca contradictionda contingency
Answers to 11.1

1. (b) — the negation of "all" is "at least one is not"; option (a) is the common over-negation.

2. (b) — a true hypothesis with a false conclusion is the only way to break an implication.

3. (c) — contrapositive negates and reverses; (a) is the converse and (b) is the inverse.

4. (c) — n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)=20+15-5=30; (b) forgets to subtract the overlap.

5. (b) — the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements.

6. (c) — a statement and its negation cannot both be true, so the conjunction is always false.

11.2 Real Numbers

  1. Which of the following is an irrational number? [1]a0.\overline{3}b\sqrt{16}c\sqrt{7}d\frac{22}{7}
  2. The solution set of |x-3|<2 is [1]a(1,5)b[1,5]c(-5,-1)d(-\infty,1)\cup(5,\infty)
  3. The solutions of |2x-1|=3 are [1]ax=2 onlybx=-1 onlycx=2 and x=-1dx=1 and x=-2
  4. [-2,3]\cap(0,5) equals [1]a(0,3)b[0,3]c(0,3]d[-2,5)
  5. The solution set of |x|\ge 4 is [1]a[-4,4]b(-4,4)c(-\infty,-4]\cup[4,\infty)d[4,\infty)
Answers to 11.2

1. (c) — 7 is not a perfect square; 0.\overline{3}=1/3 and 22/7 are rational, \sqrt{16}=4.

2. (a) — |x-3|<2 means -2<x-3<2, so 1<x<5; the strict inequality gives open ends.

3. (c) — 2x-1=3\Rightarrow x=2 and 2x-1=-3\Rightarrow x=-1; (a) forgets the negative case.

4. (c) — the common part starts after 0 (open in the second set) and ends at 3 (closed in the first).

5. (c) — "\ge" gives two outer rays; (a) is the solution of |x|\le 4.

11.3 Functions

  1. If f(x)=2x+3, then f^{-1}(x) is [1]a\frac{x+3}{2}b\frac{x-3}{2}c2x-3d\frac{2}{x-3}
  2. The domain of f(x)=\sqrt{x-4} is [1]a(4,\infty)b[4,\infty)c(-\infty,4]d\mathbb{R}
  3. If f(x)=x^2 and g(x)=x+1, then (f\circ g)(2) is [1]a5b9c7d25
  4. The range of f(x)=x^2+1 is [1]a[0,\infty)b(1,\infty)c[1,\infty)d\mathbb{R}
  5. The domain of f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2-9} is [1]a\mathbb{R}-\{3\}b\mathbb{R}-\{-3\}c\mathbb{R}-\{3,-3\}d\mathbb{R}
  6. If f(x)=\log_2 x, then f(8) equals [1]a2b3c4d16
Answers to 11.3

1. (b) — put y=2x+3 and solve for x: x=(y-3)/2.

2. (b) — we need x-4\ge 0; \sqrt{0} is defined, so 4 is included.

3. (b) — g(2)=3, then f(3)=9; (a) wrongly computes (g\circ f)(2)=5.

4. (c) — x^2\ge 0, so x^2+1\ge 1 and the value 1 is attained at x=0.

5. (c) — the denominator vanishes at both x=3 and x=-3.

6. (b) — 2^3=8.

11.4 Curve Sketching

  1. Which of the following is an even function? [1]ax^3b\sin xcx^2+\cos xdx+\frac{1}{x}
  2. The period of \sin 2x is [1]a2\pib\pic\frac{\pi}{2}d4\pi
  3. The graph of y=x^3 is symmetric about [1]athe x-axisbthe y-axiscthe origindthe line y=x
  4. The amplitude of y=3\sin 2x is [1]a2b3c6d\pi
  5. The graph of y=\frac{1}{x+2} has a vertical asymptote at [1]ax=2bx=-2cy=-2dx=0
  6. The graph of y=\ln x passes through the point [1]a(0,1)b(1,0)c(e,0)d(0,0)
Answers to 11.4

1. (c) — both x^2 and \cos x are even, so their sum is even; x^3, \sin x and x+1/x are odd.

2. (b) — the period of \sin bx is 2\pi/b=\pi; (a) forgets to divide by b.

3. (c) — (-x)^3=-x^3, so the function is odd and symmetric about the origin.

4. (b) — amplitude is |a| in a\sin bx; the 2 changes the period, not the height.

5. (b) — the denominator is zero at x=-2.

6. (b) — \ln 1=0; the graph never touches x=0.

11.5 Sequence and Series

  1. The 10th term of the A.P. 3, 7, 11, \dots is [1]a39b43c40d36
  2. The sum of the first 20 natural numbers is [1]a200b210c420d190
  3. The 5th term of the G.P. 2, 6, 18, \dots is [1]a54b162c486d90
  4. The sum to infinity of 1+\frac12+\frac14+\cdots is [1]a1b\frac32c2d\infty
  5. The G.M. of 4 and 16 is [1]a10b8c6.4d12
  6. If a, b, c are in H.P., then \frac1a,\frac1b,\frac1c are in [1]aG.P.bH.P.cA.P.dnone of these
  7. The sum of the first 15 odd natural numbers is [1]a225b240c120d255
Answers to 11.5

1. (a) — t_{10}=a+9d=3+9\times4=39; (b) uses 10d by mistake.

2. (b) — \frac{n(n+1)}{2}=\frac{20\times21}{2}=210.

3. (b) — r=3, so t_5=2\times3^4=162; (c) is t_6.

4. (c) — S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}=\frac{1}{1-1/2}=2.

5. (b) — \sqrt{4\times16}=8; (a) is the A.M. and (c) is the H.M.

6. (c) — that is the definition of a harmonic progression.

7. (a) — the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^2=225.

11.6 Matrices and Determinants

  1. For two matrices A and B for which the product is defined, (AB)^T equals [1]aA^TB^TbB^TA^TcABdBA
  2. The determinant of the matrix with rows (2,3) and (1,4) is [1]a11b5c-5d8
  3. If A is a 2\times2 matrix with |A|=5, then |2A| is [1]a10b20c25d40
  4. For a square matrix A, A\cdot\text{adj}A equals [1]aA^2b|A|\,IcIdO
  5. The inverse of a square matrix A exists if and only if [1]a|A|=0b|A|\ne 0cA is symmetricdA=A^T
  6. If A is a 3\times3 matrix with |A|=4, then |\text{adj}A| is [1]a4b8c16d64
Answers to 11.6

1. (b) — the transpose of a product reverses the order; (a) is the commonest slip.

2. (b) — 2\times4-3\times1=5.

3. (b) — for an n\times n matrix |kA|=k^n|A|, so 2^2\times5=20; (a) multiplies once only.

4. (b) — A\,\text{adj}A=|A|I, the identity behind the inverse formula.

5. (b) — a singular matrix (|A|=0) has no inverse.

6. (c) — |\text{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}=4^2=16.

11.7 Quadratic Equation

  1. The roots of x^2-5x+6=0 are [1]a1, 6b2, 3c-2,-3d-1,-6
  2. The nature of the roots of 2x^2-4x+2=0 is [1]areal and distinctbreal and equalcimaginarydirrational
  3. The sum and product of the roots of 2x^2-7x+3=0 are [1]a\frac72,\frac32b-\frac72,\frac32c\frac72,-\frac32d7,3
  4. The quadratic equation whose roots are 2 and -3 is [1]ax^2-x-6=0bx^2+x-6=0cx^2+x+6=0dx^2-5x-6=0
  5. If the roots of x^2+kx+9=0 are equal, then k is [1]a6 onlyb-6 onlyc\pm6d\pm3
  6. If \alpha,\beta are the roots of x^2-4x+1=0, then \alpha^2+\beta^2 is [1]a16b14c18d12
Answers to 11.7

1. (b) — (x-2)(x-3)=0; (c) has the wrong signs.

2. (b) — D=16-16=0, so the roots are real and equal.

3. (a) — sum =-b/a=7/2, product =c/a=3/2; (b) forgets the minus sign in -b/a.

4. (b) — sum =-1, product =-6, so x^2-(\text{sum})x+\text{product}=x^2+x-6.

5. (c) — D=k^2-36=0 gives k=\pm6; both signs work.

6. (b) — \alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=16-2=14.

11.8 Complex Numbers

  1. The value of i^{46} is [1]a1b-1cid-i
  2. (2+3i)(2-3i) equals [1]a-5b13c4-9id7
  3. The modulus of 3+4i is [1]a7b25c5d1
  4. The square roots of -3+4i are [1]a\pm(1+2i)b\pm(2+i)c1-2i onlyd\pm(2-i)
  5. The conjugate of \frac{1}{1+i} is [1]a\frac{1-i}{2}b\frac{1+i}{2}c1-id\frac{1}{1-i} only
  6. The argument of the complex number -1 is [1]a0b\frac{\pi}{2}c\pid\frac{3\pi}{2}
Answers to 11.8

1. (b) — 46=4\times11+2, so i^{46}=i^2=-1.

2. (b) — z\bar z=a^2+b^2=4+9=13; (c) forgets i^2=-1.

3. (c) — \sqrt{9+16}=5; (b) is |z|^2.

4. (a) — (1+2i)^2=1-4+4i=-3+4i; both \pm roots are needed, and (c) leaves out the other one.

5. (b) — \frac{1}{1+i}=\frac{1-i}{2}, whose conjugate is \frac{1+i}{2}; (a) stops one step short.

6. (c) — the point -1 lies on the negative real axis, angle \pi.

11.9 Inverse Circular Functions

  1. \sin^{-1}\left(\frac12\right) is [1]a\frac{\pi}{3}b\frac{\pi}{6}c\frac{\pi}{4}d\frac{5\pi}{6}
  2. The range (principal values) of \cos^{-1}x is [1]a[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}]b[0,\pi]c(0,\pi)d[0,2\pi]
  3. \sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x equals, for -1\le x\le 1, [1]a0b\pic\frac{\pi}{2}d\frac{\pi}{4}
  4. \tan^{-1}\frac12+\tan^{-1}\frac13 equals [1]a\frac{\pi}{6}b\frac{\pi}{3}c\frac{\pi}{4}d\frac{\pi}{2}
  5. \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right) is [1]a\frac{\pi}{3}b-\frac{\pi}{3}c\frac{2\pi}{3}d\frac{4\pi}{3}
  6. \sin\left(\cos^{-1}\frac35\right) equals [1]a\frac35b\frac45c\frac34d\frac53
Answers to 11.9

1. (b) — principal value in [-\pi/2,\pi/2]; 5\pi/6 also has sine \frac12 but is outside the range.

2. (b) — \cos^{-1} takes values in [0,\pi]; (a) is the range of \sin^{-1}.

3. (c) — the standard complementary identity.

4. (c) — \tan^{-1}\frac{\frac12+\frac13}{1-\frac16}=\tan^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{4}.

5. (c) — \cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x=\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}; (b) lies outside [0,\pi].

6. (b) — a 3-4-5 triangle: if the cosine is 3/5, the sine is 4/5.

11.10 Trigonometric Equations and General Values

  1. The general solution of \sin x=\frac12 is [1]a2n\pi\pm\frac{\pi}{6}bn\pi+(-1)^n\frac{\pi}{6}cn\pi\pm\frac{\pi}{6}dn\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}
  2. The general solution of \cos x=0 is [1]an\pib2n\pic(2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2}dn\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}
  3. The general solution of \tan x=\sqrt{3} is [1]an\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}b2n\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}cn\pi\pm\frac{\pi}{3}dn\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}
  4. The number of solutions of \sin x=\frac12 in [0,2\pi] is [1]a1b2c3d4
  5. If \cos x=\cos\alpha, then the general value of x is [1]an\pi+\alphabn\pi+(-1)^n\alphac2n\pi\pm\alphad2n\pi+\alpha
  6. The smallest positive solution of \tan x=-1 is [1]a\frac{\pi}{4}b\frac{3\pi}{4}c\frac{5\pi}{4}d\frac{7\pi}{4}
Answers to 11.10

1. (b) — for \sin x=\sin\alpha the general value is n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha with \alpha=\pi/6.

2. (c) — cosine vanishes at odd multiples of \pi/2; (a) is the answer for \sin x=0.

3. (a) — tangent has period \pi, so n\pi+\alpha with \alpha=\pi/3.

4. (b) — x=\frac{\pi}{6} and x=\frac{5\pi}{6}.

5. (c) — cosine repeats every 2\pi and is even, hence \pm\alpha.

6. (b) — tangent is negative in the second quadrant; the reference angle is \pi/4, giving \pi-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{3\pi}{4}.

11.11 Straight Line

  1. The perpendicular distance of the point (2,1) from the line 3x+4y+5=0 is [1]a3b5c\frac{15}{25}d15
  2. The distance of the origin from the line 5x+12y-26=0 is [1]a26b13c2d1
  3. The equations of the bisectors of the angles between the coordinate axes are [1]ay=0 and x=0by=\pm xcy=\pm 2xdx+y=1
  4. The distance of the point (-1,3) from the line x+y=0 is [1]a2b\sqrt{2}c2\sqrt{2}d1
  5. The two bisectors of the angles between two intersecting straight lines are [1]aparallelbperpendicular to each otherccoincidentdinclined at 45^\circ always
Answers to 11.11

1. (a) — \frac{|3(2)+4(1)+5|}{\sqrt{9+16}}=\frac{15}{5}=3; (c) forgets the square root.

2. (c) — \frac{|-26|}{\sqrt{25+144}}=\frac{26}{13}=2.

3. (b) — the axes are perpendicular, so the bisectors make 45^\circ with each: y=\pm x.

4. (b) — \frac{|-1+3|}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}; (a) forgets to divide by \sqrt{2}.

5. (b) — the internal and external bisectors always meet at a right angle.

11.12 Pair of Straight Lines

  1. The equation x^2-y^2=0 represents [1]aa circlebthe lines y=x and y=-xcone linedparallel lines
  2. The angle between the lines x^2-5xy+6y^2=0 has \tan\theta equal to [1]a\frac17b\frac15c1d\frac{1}{6}
  3. The lines given by ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0 are perpendicular if [1]ah=0ba=bca+b=0dab=h^2
  4. The lines given by ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0 coincide if [1]ah^2=abbh=0ca+b=0da=b
  5. A homogeneous equation of the second degree in x and y represents a pair of lines [1]aparallel to the axesbpassing through the origincnot intersectingdof equal slope
  6. The equation of the bisectors of ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0 is [1]a\frac{x^2-y^2}{a-b}=\frac{xy}{h}b\frac{x^2+y^2}{a+b}=\frac{xy}{h}c\frac{x^2-y^2}{a+b}=\frac{xy}{h}d\frac{x^2-y^2}{a-b}=\frac{xy}{a}
Answers to 11.12

1. (b) — (x-y)(x+y)=0.

2. (a) — a=1,\ h=-\frac52,\ b=6; \tan\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{h^2-ab}}{|a+b|}=\frac{2\times\frac12}{7}=\frac17.

3. (c) — the angle formula has a+b in the denominator; perpendicular means that denominator is zero.

4. (a) — h^2-ab=0 makes the numerator of \tan\theta zero, so the angle is zero.

5. (b) — with no linear or constant term the origin satisfies the equation.

6. (a) — the standard result; (b) and (c) mix up the signs.

11.13 Coordinates in Space

  1. The distance between (1,2,3) and (4,6,15) is [1]a11b12c13d14
  2. The direction cosines of the x-axis are [1]a(0,1,0)b(1,0,0)c(0,0,1)d(1,1,1)
  3. The distance of the point (3,-4,5) from the xy-plane is [1]a3b4c5d\sqrt{50}
  4. The direction cosines of the line joining (1,2,3) and (3,5,9) are [1]a\frac27,\frac37,\frac67b\frac13,\frac13,\frac13c2,3,6d\frac{2}{49},\frac{3}{49},\frac{6}{49}
  5. Which of the following can be the direction cosines of a line? [1]a\frac12,\frac12,\frac12b\frac13,\frac23,\frac23c\frac12,\frac13,\frac14d1,1,1
  6. The distance of the point (2,-3,6) from the origin is [1]a5b6c7d11
Answers to 11.13

1. (c) — \sqrt{3^2+4^2+12^2}=\sqrt{169}=13.

2. (b) — the x-axis makes 0^\circ with itself and 90^\circ with the others.

3. (c) — the distance from the xy-plane is |z|.

4. (a) — direction ratios 2,3,6 with \sqrt{4+9+36}=7; (c) leaves the ratios unnormalised.

5. (b) — only (b) satisfies l^2+m^2+n^2=\frac19+\frac49+\frac49=1.

6. (c) — \sqrt{4+9+36}=7.

11.14 Vectors

  1. Which pair of vectors is collinear? [1]a2\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j} and -\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}b\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} and \mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}c\mathbf{i} and \mathbf{j}d2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} and \mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}
  2. The value of m for which 2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j} and 4\mathbf{i}+m\mathbf{j} are collinear is [1]a4b5c6d8
  3. Two non-collinear vectors \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b} are linearly independent; if x\mathbf{a}+y\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0} then [1]ax=y=0bx=y=1cx=-ydx=0 only
  4. The position vector of the midpoint of the points with position vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} is [1]a\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}b\frac{\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}}{2}c\frac{\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}}{2}d\frac{2\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}}{3}
  5. The magnitude of 3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j} is [1]a7b5c25d1
  6. Three vectors are coplanar if [1]athey are all unit vectorsbone of them is a linear combination of the other twocthey are mutually perpendiculardthey have equal magnitudes
Answers to 11.14

1. (a) — the second is -\frac12 times the first; the others have unequal component ratios.

2. (c) — \frac24=\frac3m gives m=6.

3. (a) — that is the definition of linear independence.

4. (c) — the midpoint formula is the average of the position vectors.

5. (b) — \sqrt{9+16}=5; (a) adds the components.

6. (b) — that is the condition for coplanarity.

11.15 Measures of Dispersion

  1. The variance of the data 1,2,3,4,5 is [1]a1b2c2.5d3
  2. The coefficient of variation is defined as [1]a\frac{\bar x}{\sigma}\times100b\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100c\sigma^2\times100d\frac{\sigma}{\sigma^2}
  3. If the mean is 50 and the standard deviation is 5, the coefficient of variation is [1]a10%b5%c25%d50%
  4. Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness is [1]a\frac{\text{Mean}-\text{Mode}}{\text{S.D.}}b\frac{\text{Mean}+\text{Mode}}{\text{S.D.}}c\frac{\text{S.D.}}{\text{Mean}-\text{Mode}}d\text{Mean}-\text{Median}
  5. If the mean is 40, the mode 30 and the S.D. 10, the coefficient of skewness is [1]a-1b0c1d3
  6. The skewness of a perfectly symmetrical distribution is [1]apositivebnegativeczerodinfinite
Answers to 11.15

1. (b) — mean 3, squared deviations 4+1+0+1+4=10, divide by n=5 to get 2; (c) wrongly divides by n-1.

2. (b) — C.V. =\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%; (a) is inverted.

3. (a) — \frac{5}{50}\times100=10\%.

4. (a) — the mean minus the mode, divided by the standard deviation.

5. (c) — \frac{40-30}{10}=1, positive skew.

6. (c) — mean, median and mode coincide, so the numerator is zero.

11.16 Probability

  1. A fair die is thrown. The probability of getting a prime number is [1]a\frac13b\frac12c\frac23d\frac16
  2. For two events, P(A\cup B) equals [1]aP(A)+P(B)bP(A)P(B)cP(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)dP(A)-P(B)
  3. If A and B are independent with P(A)=0.3 and P(B)=0.4, then P(A\cap B) is [1]a0.7b0.1c0.12d0.58
  4. Two coins are tossed. The probability of at least one head is [1]a\frac14b\frac12c\frac34d1
  5. The probability of drawing a king or a queen from a pack of 52 cards is [1]a\frac{1}{13}b\frac{2}{13}c\frac{1}{26}d\frac{4}{13}
  6. Two dice are thrown. The probability that the sum is 7 is [1]a\frac{1}{12}b\frac{1}{9}c\frac16d\frac{7}{36}
Answers to 11.16

1. (b) — primes 2,3,5: \frac36=\frac12; the trap is counting 1 as prime.

2. (c) — the addition law; (a) double-counts the overlap.

3. (c) — independence gives 0.3\times0.4=0.12; (a) adds instead.

4. (c) — 1-P(\text{no head})=1-\frac14.

5. (b) — \frac{4+4}{52}=\frac{2}{13} (mutually exclusive events add).

6. (c) — six favourable outcomes out of 36.

11.17 Limits and Continuity

  1. \lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2} equals [1]a0b2c4ddoes not exist
  2. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin3x}{x} equals [1]a1b3c\frac13d0
  3. \lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x+1}{x+5} equals [1]a0b1c3d\infty
  4. \lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x} equals [1]a0b1ced\infty
  5. \lim_{x\to\infty}\left(1+\frac1x\right)^x equals [1]a1b0ced\infty
  6. The function f(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} for x\ne 1, f(1)=k, is continuous at x=1 when k is [1]a0b1c2d-2
Answers to 11.17

1. (c) — factorise: \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2\to4; it is the \frac00 form, not "does not exist".

2. (b) — \frac{\sin3x}{x}=3\cdot\frac{\sin3x}{3x}\to3; (a) forgets the factor 3.

3. (c) — divide by x: the ratio of leading coefficients 3/1.

4. (b) — a standard limit.

5. (c) — the definition of e; (a) is the trap of putting \frac1x\to0 first.

6. (c) — the limit is x+1\to2, so continuity needs f(1)=2.

11.18 Derivatives

Chapter summary

  • Group A is eleven one-mark MCQs; they are spread across algebra, trigonometry, geometry, vectors, statistics, calculus and the computational-or-mechanics unit.
  • Logic: the contrapositive of p\Rightarrow q is \sim q\Rightarrow\sim p; n(A\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B).
  • Algebra: t_n=a+(n-1)d, S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}, \alpha+\beta=-\frac ba, \alpha\beta=\frac ca, |kA|=k^n|A|, |\text{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}, |z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.
  • Trigonometry: \sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}; general values n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha, 2n\pi\pm\alpha, n\pi+\alpha.
  • Geometry: distance =\frac{|ax_1+by_1+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}; a pair of lines is perpendicular when a+b=0; l^2+m^2+n^2=1.
  • Statistics and probability: C.V. =\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100; P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
  • Calculus: \int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx=\ln|f(x)|; standard limits \frac{\sin x}{x}\to1 and \frac{e^x-1}{x}\to1.
  • Computational methods: x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}; Simpson's rule needs an even number of intervals.
